asset-liability-management.definition: Managing the match between a bank's assets and liabilities to reduce funding liquidity risk; it lies at the heart of the banking business.
asset-liability-management.name: Asset/Liability Management

audit-committee.definition: A committee of the board of directors. Under SOX the names of its members must be disclosed, and they are expected to understand accounting principles and financial statements and to have experience with internal audits.
audit-committee.name: Audit Committee

basel-accords-evolution.definition: How the Basel Committee's capital framework moved from Basel I's simple risk-weighted 8% minimum to Basel II's refined weightings and then to Basel III's post-crisis focus on capital quality and liquidity.

value: Basel I (1988): risk-weighted capital requirements with minimum capital at 8% of risk-weighted assets
Basel II (set 2006): kept the 8%, refined risk weighting, added trading activity and became more attuned to financial innovation
Basel III: higher capital quality (core Tier 1 limited to common equity and retained earnings), new LCR and NSFR liquidity ratios, and a macroprudential overlay
The framework was revised again in 2016 with the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB)

basel-accords-evolution.name: Evolution of the Basel Accords

basel-committee.definition: A group of big-country banking regulators who get together to set shared "best practice" rules for banks.
basel-committee.name: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision

basel-i.definition: The 1988 Basel Accord, which set capital adequacy standards after the Latin American debt crisis using a risk-weighted approach, with minimum capital at 8% of a firm's risk-weighted assets.
basel-i.name: Basel I

basel-ii.definition: The BCBS revision of the capital adequacy framework (begun in 1999, set in 2006) that superseded Basel I. It kept the 8% minimum but refined the risk weighting and added trading activity alongside lending activity.
basel-ii.name: Basel II

basel-iii.definition: The post-crisis Basel framework, with a big emphasis on capital adequacy. It raised capital quality by limiting core Tier 1 capital to common equity and retained earnings, and imposed new short- and long-term liquidity ratios.
basel-iii.name: Basel III

basel-iii-macroprudential-overlay.definition: The set of five system-wide elements added in Basel III in response to the financial crisis.

value: A leverage ratio of 3%
A countercyclical capital buffer
Total loss-absorbing capital (TLAC) standards for global systemically important banks (G-SIBs)
Systemically important markets and infrastructures (SIMIs), e.g. moving OTC derivatives to central clearing and trade reporting
Capturing systemic risk and tail events in risk modeling and stress testing

basel-iii-macroprudential-overlay.name: Basel III Macroprudential Overlay

brainstorming-and-triaging-risks.definition: Techniques for gathering information about the risks a firm faces and judging their frequency and severity.

value: Brainstorming: discussions with representatives from different business divisions about their exposures
Structured interviews with professionals inside or outside the company
Industry resources: checklists, professional and regulatory standards, industry surveys
Loss data analysis: frequency and severity of loss events and how they relate to risk factors
Basic risk triage: not every risk is quantifiable, but its frequency and severity can be judged
What-if analysis of worst-case scenarios
Include front-line staff in risk information gathering
Follow the trail of key processes to find weaknesses or gaps

brainstorming-and-triaging-risks.name: Brainstorming and Triaging Risks

business-risk.definition: Risk arising from day-to-day business matters such as customer demand, pricing decisions, supplier negotiations, competition and product innovation.
business-risk.name: Business Risk

collar.definition: A hedge that combines call and put options.

value: Airlines use collars, alongside swaps and call options, to hedge jet fuel prices

collar.name: Collar

collateralized.definition: Backed by something valuable that the lender can take if the borrower doesn't pay.
collateralized.name: Collateralized

commodity-price-risk.definition: The chance you lose money because the prices of raw materials (commodities) suddenly change.

value: Hedging jet fuel with crude oil futures can fail if the historical relationship between the two prices breaks down

commodity-price-risk.name: Commodity Price Risk

comply-or-explain.definition: The approach England took instead of SOX-style legislation, relying on corporate governance codes and a regime of "comply or explain".
comply-or-explain.name: Comply or Explain

comprehensive-capital-analysis-and-revie.definition: The Federal Reserve's annual stress testing exercise for large banks, in which a BHC presents a capital plan over a nine-quarter horizon under supervisory and internally generated scenarios.
comprehensive-capital-analysis-and-revie.name: Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review

consumer-financial-protection-bureau.definition: The agency created by Dodd-Frank to regulate consumer financial services and products.
consumer-financial-protection-bureau.name: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau

corporate-hedging-pitfalls.definition: Almost everything can go wrong with corporate hedging, from misunderstanding the exposure to poor communication about how the hedge behaves.

value: Misunderstanding or incorrectly mapping the risk exposure
Failing to notice changes in market structure
Suffering from a rogue trader on the team
Poor communication can cause a major breakdown
MGRM in 1993 promised 150 million barrels of gasoline and heating oil at fixed prices over ten years; falling prices caused massive margin calls and a liquidity drain
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of hedging and the challenges of implementing a hedging strategy

corporate-hedging-pitfalls.name: What Can Go Wrong with Corporate Hedging

countercyclical-capital-buffer.definition: A capital buffer that is one of the five elements of the Basel III macroprudential overlay.
countercyclical-capital-buffer.name: Countercyclical Capital Buffer

credit-risk.definition: The failure of one party to fulfill its financial obligations to another party. It is driven by the probability of default, the exposure amount at default, and the amount that can be recovered.

value: A debtor fails to pay interest or principal on a loan (bankruptcy or default risk)
An obligor or counterparty is downgraded (downgrade risk)
A counterparty to a market trade fails to perform, including settlement (Herstatt) risk

credit-risk.name: Credit Risk

default-risk.definition: The risk that a debtor fails to pay interest or principal on a loan.
default-risk.name: Default Risk

delta.definition: An option greek: the sensitivity of option value to a change in the value of the underlying.
delta.name: Delta

derivatives-market.definition: A global financial market where standardized and customized derivative contracts such as futures, options, swaps and forwards are traded. It grew rapidly across two decades.
derivatives-market.name: Derivatives Market

dodd-frank-act.definition: A US regulatory response to the 2007-2009 financial crisis.
dodd-frank-act.name: Dodd-Frank Act

dodd-frank-act-reforms.definition: The 2010 US law aimed at consumer protection and systemic stability, passed after the crisis exposed that investment banks sat outside prudential bank regulation.

value: In 1999 the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act removed the Glass-Steagall restrictions, but commercial and investment banking stayed under two separate regulatory paradigms
Investment banking was not under the purview of bank regulators, so it was not subject to prudential oversight
In the crisis Bear Stearns and Merrill Lynch were absorbed in mergers, Lehman Brothers went bankrupt, and Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley converted into bank holding companies (BHCs)
Strengthened the Fed, which now regulates all SIFIs (bank holding firms with more than USD 50 billion in assets)
Replaced "too big to fail" with an orderly liquidation authority (OLA)
Requires SIFIs to submit a resolution plan ("living will") to the Fed and the FDIC
Launched a transparency-focused overhaul of derivatives markets to help participants with counterparty risk
The Volcker Rule bans proprietary trading and hedge fund or private equity ownership by banking entities; the 2018 reform would exempt banks under USD 10 billion in assets
Created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
Introduced a new approach to scenario analysis and stress testing

dodd-frank-act-reforms.name: Dodd-Frank Act Reforms

dodd-frank-act-stress-test.definition: One of the two Federal Reserve stress testing exercises, for banks with assets above USD 10 billion.
dodd-frank-act-stress-test.name: Dodd-Frank Act Stress Test

dodd-frank-stress-testing.definition: The radically new approach to scenario analysis and stress testing that Dodd-Frank introduced, run by the Federal Reserve through DFAST and CCAR.

value: Top-down, with macroeconomic scenarios unfolding over several quarters
Looks at how macroeconomic downturns affect credit, liquidity, market and operational risk
Computationally demanding, because risk drivers are not stationary and portfolios can be actively managed
Fully built into a bank's business, capital and liquidity planning
Looks across all institutions, not just each bank alone, to show how a common scenario would hit the largest banks together
DFAST covers banks with assets above USD 10 billion; CCAR covers banks above USD 50 billion
CCAR is annual, with three supervisory scenarios and two internal ones (BHC baseline and BHC adverse)
Under CCAR a BHC presents a capital plan of planned actions (dividend increases, share repurchases, major acquisitions) over 9 quarters and must keep a Tier 1 capital ratio of at least 4.5%
Since the 2018 reform, CCAR is mandatory only for banks with assets above USD 250 billion

dodd-frank-stress-testing.name: Dodd-Frank Stress Testing Approach

downgrade-risk.definition: The risk that an obligor or counterparty is downgraded, signalling higher risk that may lead to an immediate loss in value of a credit-linked security.
downgrade-risk.name: Downgrade Risk

duration-analysis.definition: An ALM technique, alongside gap analysis, for checking whether a firm's money is lined up correctly over time.
duration-analysis.name: Duration Analysis

eba-stress-test.definition: The stress test EU banks with assets of 30 billion or more must run. Its scenarios unfold over three years and it is fundamentally static, looking only at the immediate impact of the cumulative shocks.
eba-stress-test.name: EBA Stress Test

economic-capital.definition: The amount of capital the firm requires based on its understanding of its economic risks; it should be large enough to absorb unexpected losses. Not the same as regulatory capital.
economic-capital.name: Economic Capital

equity-risk.definition: The chance that you can lose money because stock prices go down.

value: A stock worth $100 falls to $80; the $20 difference is equity risk

equity-risk.name: Equity Risk

european-regulatory-response.definition: Europe's post-crisis supervisory regime, built around the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) and EBA stress tests.

value: SREP principle: a forward-looking focus on the sustainability of each bank's business model, including under stress
SREP principle: an assessment methodology based on industry best practices
SREP principle: every bank will ultimately operate under the same standards
ICAAP and ILAAP are the two key components of SREP
EU banks with assets of 30 billion or more must run EBA stress tests
Compared with CCAR, EBA scenarios unfold over three years and are fundamentally static, looking only at the immediate impact of the cumulative shocks

european-regulatory-response.name: European Regulatory Response to the GFC

expected-loss.definition: The average loss a position taker might expect to incur from a position or portfolio. It is a function of the probability of the risk event, the firm's exposure to it, and the severity of the loss if it occurs.
expected-loss.name: Expected Loss

expected-shortfall.definition: For a given tail probability, the average of the losses beyond the VaR at that probability. It addresses VaR's failure to quantify risk in the tail of the loss distribution.
expected-shortfall.name: Expected Shortfall

exposure-at-default.definition: The exposure amount at the time of default; one of the levers that drives credit risk.
exposure-at-default.name: Exposure at Default

extreme-value-theory.definition: A statistical technique used to identify tail risk events.
extreme-value-theory.name: Extreme Value Theory

forward-contract.definition: A customized contract between two parties to buy or sell an asset at a specified price on a future date. Unlike futures, forwards trade over the counter rather than on a centralized exchange, which brings a higher risk of default.
forward-contract.name: Forward Contract

fundamental-review-of-the-trading-book.definition: The 2016 revision of the Basel framework.
fundamental-review-of-the-trading-book.name: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book

funding-liquidity-risk.definition: The risk that a firm cannot access enough liquid cash and assets to meet its obligations.

value: Start-ups that find it difficult to pay bills quickly while also funding future endeavors
Banks taking short-term deposits and lending the money out for the longer term (a funding mismatch)

funding-liquidity-risk.name: Funding Liquidity Risk

futures-contract.definition: A derivative contract that obligates the parties to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined future date and price. Futures trade on exchanges.

value: Stock market futures obligate the buyer to purchase and the seller to sell a stock or set of stocks at a set future date and price
Busch could fix the price it pays per bushel of wheat using wheat futures traded on the CBOT

futures-contract.name: Futures Contract

gap-analysis.definition: A simple way for a bank (or any company) to check whether money coming in and money going out are lined up over time, so it doesn't run out of cash when bills are due.
gap-analysis.name: Gap Analysis

general-market-risk.definition: The risk that an asset class will fall in value, leading to a fall in the value of an individual asset or portfolio.
general-market-risk.name: General Market Risk

global-financial-crisis-causes.definition: The crisis followed a downturn in a previously hot housing market fuelled by easy mortgages and accelerated by a booming market for mortgage-backed securities traded by financial institutions.

value: Credit markets were defined by low underwriting standards, no oversight and reliance on complex credit instruments
Basel II was being implemented right before the crisis

global-financial-crisis-causes.name: Causes of the 2007-2009 Financial Crisis

gramm-leach-bliley-act.definition: The 1999 US act that abolished the restrictions of the Glass-Steagall Act, letting bank holding companies convert into financial services holding companies (FSHCs).
gramm-leach-bliley-act.name: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act

hedging-philosophy.definition: Just because a risk can be hedged does not mean it should be; hedging is intended to reduce the chance of financial distress but has both transparent and opaque costs.

value: Costs can be transparent (option premiums) or opaque (tactical errors, rogue trading)
Theoretical arguments against hedging assume perfect, frictionless markets, but there are many imperfections
Hedging can increase cash flows, e.g. letting a firm offer customers a stable price by hedging a key cost input
Equity investors concentrated in one firm generally want managers to hedge; diversified investors generally do not
Risk management instruments can themselves have negative consequences
A firm hit by an unexpected market loss tends to cut investment in other areas and move more cautiously
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of hedging and the challenges of implementing a hedging strategy

hedging-philosophy.name: Hedging Philosophy

herstatt-risk.definition: The risk that a counterparty to a market trade fails to perform at settlement: "paid first, didn't receive later". Named after the Herstatt bank in Germany.
herstatt-risk.name: Herstatt Risk

interest-rate-and-fx-risk-management.definition: Managing interest rate and foreign currency exposures, one of the more important areas of price risk management for many firms.

value: Business activities often create natural hedges, such as inflows and outflows of the same foreign currency
A firm balances interest rate risk through its financial risk appetite, which can set the level of debt the board accepts
It also sets the proportion of fixed to variable interest rate debt
Interest rate changes are linked to the broader economy and consumer demand and can affect a firm's ability to meet its debt obligations
Apply appropriate methods to hedge operational and financial risks, including foreign currency and interest rate risk

interest-rate-and-fx-risk-management.name: Interest Rate and Foreign Exchange Risk Management

interest-rate-risk.definition: Rates can move, and that can hurt financially.

value: If rates go up, the value of many existing bonds usually goes down, because new bonds pay higher interest
A loan with a variable (floating) rate has higher payments when rates rise
If rates go down, old bonds can be worth more and variable-rate loan payments can fall

interest-rate-risk.name: Interest Rate Risk

internal-capital-adequacy-assessment-pro.definition: One of the two key components of SREP. It incorporates scenario analysis and stress testing, showing how stress testing supports capital planning.
internal-capital-adequacy-assessment-pro.name: Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process

internal-liquidity-adequacy-assessment-p.definition: One of the two key components of SREP. It incorporates the potential losses from asset liquidation and higher funding costs during stressful periods.
internal-liquidity-adequacy-assessment-p.name: Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process

key-performance-indicator.definition: A metric that tracks some performance factor associated with risk.
key-performance-indicator.name: Key Performance Indicator

key-risk-indicator.definition: A metric that tracks some factor closely associated with risk.
key-risk-indicator.name: Key Risk Indicator

leverage-ratio.definition: A minimum leverage ratio of 3%, one of the five elements of the Basel III macroprudential overlay.
leverage-ratio.name: Leverage Ratio

liquidity-coverage-ratio.definition: A 30-day, short-term liquidity ratio imposed by Basel III.
liquidity-coverage-ratio.name: Liquidity Coverage Ratio

liquidity-risk.definition: Liquidity risk is really two separate kinds of risk: funding liquidity risk and market (trading) liquidity risk.
liquidity-risk.name: Liquidity Risk

living-will.definition: A resolution plan that SIFIs must submit to the Federal Reserve and the FDIC, laying out a corporate governance structure for resolution planning.
living-will.name: Living Will

loss-given-default.definition: The severity of the loss if a default occurs, which depends on the amount that can be recovered.
loss-given-default.name: Loss Given Default

market-liquidity-risk.definition: The risk of a loss in asset value when markets temporarily seize up, which may force a seller to accept an abnormally low price or leave them unable to turn an asset into cash at any price.
market-liquidity-risk.name: Market Liquidity Risk

market-risk.definition: The change in market prices can drive the value of securities and other assets up and down. Price volatility is the engine of market risk. Depending on the underlying asset, risk can take different forms such as Equity Risk, Interest Rate Risk, Currency Risk and Commodity Price Risk.
market-risk.name: Market Risk

modern-imperative-to-manage-risk.definition: Firms manage their core business risks out of a mix of need and opportunity: markets liberalized in the 1970s, and new risk management instruments followed in the 1980s and 1990s.

value: Need: liberalization of commodity, interest rate, credit and foreign exchange markets in the 1970s increased price volatility
Opportunity: market growth in the 1980s and 1990s spawned risk management instruments, helped by the Black-Scholes-Merton model and securitization
Credit and weather derivatives were introduced
The principal derivatives markets grew rapidly across two decades

modern-imperative-to-manage-risk.name: The Modern Imperative to Manage Risk

natural-hedge.definition: An offset that arises from a firm's normal business activities rather than from a hedging instrument, such as matching inflows and outflows of the same foreign currency.
natural-hedge.name: Natural Hedge

net-stable-funding-ratio.definition: A one-year, long-term liquidity ratio imposed by Basel III.
net-stable-funding-ratio.name: Net Stable Funding Ratio

notional-value.definition: The total value of the underlying asset in a derivative contract or leveraged position. Notional values are higher than market values because leverage amplifies how much of the market a position controls.

value: Notional limits, one of the risk limit types a firm can set, cap positions by notional value

notional-value.name: Notional Value

operational-risk.definition: The risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems or from external events. Includes legal risk, but excludes business, strategic and reputational risk.

value: Anti-money laundering risk
Cyber risk
Terrorist attacks
Rogue trading

operational-risk.name: Operational Risk

option.definition: A financial instrument whose value is based on the value of underlying securities such as stocks.
option.name: Option

orderly-liquidation-authority.definition: The mechanism Dodd-Frank created to replace "too big to fail", so a failing firm can be wound down in an orderly way.
orderly-liquidation-authority.name: Orderly Liquidation Authority

over-the-counter.definition: A private bilateral agreement between two parties rather than an instrument offered through one of the large exchanges. OTC and exchange-based derivatives have different strengths and weaknesses, particularly for liquidity and counterparty credit risk.
over-the-counter.name: Over-the-Counter

value.meaning: standard normal quantile at confidence α

value: Returns are normally distributed
Portfolio value is linear in the risk factor

value.horizon: σ and μ are measured over the VaR horizon
value.sign: VaR is reported as a positive loss

parametric-var.name: Parametric (delta-normal) VaR
parametric-var.source: GARP FRM Part I, Book 4: Valuation and Risk Models, 2025 ed., ch. N, p. N

post-crisis-regulatory-response.definition: The regulatory and corporate governance changes that followed the 2007-2009 financial crisis, led by the Basel Committee's Basel III framework alongside national and regional regimes.

value: Basel III and its macroprudential overlay
Basel Committee corporate governance principles for banks, revised in 2015, focus on the board's active role in oversight and risk governance
Other responses included the US Dodd-Frank Act and the European Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP)
Explain changes in regulations and corporate risk governance that occurred as a result of the 2007-2009 financial crisis

post-crisis-regulatory-response.name: Post-Crisis Regulatory Response

probability-of-default.definition: The likelihood that the obligor or counterparty defaults; one of the levers that drives credit risk. It is assessed through risk factors such as key financial ratios, industry sector and obligor concentration.
probability-of-default.name: Probability of Default

raroc.definition: A measure banks use to factor in the cost of both expected and unexpected losses, comparing reward (after-tax net risk-adjusted expected return) to risk (economic capital).

value: To add shareholder value, RAROC should be higher than the cost of equity capital
Business comparison: compare business lines with varying levels of economic capital
Investment analysis: use projected numbers to assess likely returns from future investments
Pricing strategies: re-examine pricing for different customer segments
Risk management and cost-benefit analysis: compare the cost of risk management
Interpret the relationship between risk and reward

raroc.name: Risk-Adjusted Return on Capital

reputation-risk.definition: The danger that a firm will suffer a sudden fall in its market standing or brand with economic consequences. It typically comes from the failure of another area of risk.

value: A firm misrepresents a product's risks and loses important customers
A bank loses the trust of a regulator and is heavily criticized or curtailed

reputation-risk.name: Reputation Risk

reverse-stress-testing.definition: Starts from how bad losses could get and then works backward.
reverse-stress-testing.name: Reverse Stress Testing

rightsizing-risk-management.definition: Matching the sophistication and cost of the risk management function to the firm's strategy. A one-off hedge or an annual insurance purchase is simple; a dynamic hedging strategy with continual readjustment is a big investment.

value: Start from the risk appetite and hedging philosophy, and set basic goals such as reducing volatility, taxes or limit-breach risk
Decide the accounting treatment (cost center, economic center or profit center) and the time horizons
Right-size resources and budget, set reporting lines, accountability, oversight and independence
Establish documented policies and procedures, and evaluate performance, including incentive compensation
Dynamic strategies need more complex models and metrics
Each year, run a board-level gap analysis to check that sophistication matches the conservatism of the strategy
Decide whether risk management costs should be distributed proportionally to the areas it serves
Assess the impact of risk management tools and instruments, including risk limits and derivatives

rightsizing-risk-management.name: Rightsizing Risk Management

risk-aggregation.definition: Combining risk exposures across positions and markets into a common measure, which is difficult because specialist measures do not add up.

value: Option greeks such as delta and theta cannot be added together and do not imply the same risk across markets
VaR is a popular aggregation method but has shortcomings, notably ignoring tail risk
Expected shortfall, stress testing and reverse stress testing were responses after the crisis
Describe challenges in aggregating risk exposures

risk-aggregation.name: Risk Aggregation

risk-appetite.definition: The amount and types of risk a firm is willing to accept. Conceptually it is the firm's identity: who are we, and what do our stakeholders think we are?

value: Not the same as risk capacity, the maximum amount of risk a firm can absorb
Has two parts, a statement of willingness to take risk and the mechanisms linking it to day-to-day risk management
The banking industry is at the forefront of formalizing risk appetite because of multiple crises
Firms are typically considered either conservative or entrepreneurial in their risk profile
The industry is making risk appetite more explicit to boards and adding quantitative risk metrics
HSBC's framework used 13 key categories, including earnings, capital, liquidity, credit, traded and operational risk
Explain the relationship between risk appetite and a firm's risk management decisions

risk-appetite.name: Risk Appetite

risk-capacity.definition: The maximum amount of risk a firm can absorb. Not the same as risk appetite.
risk-capacity.name: Risk Capacity

risk-capital-allocation.definition: How a bank decides to split up a safety cushion of money across different kinds of risks.
risk-capital-allocation.name: Risk Capital Allocation

risk-governance.definition: How firms undertake and oversee risk management. It has shifted to a well-defined set of best practices and become a central tenet of modern banking regulation.

value: Driven by failures at Enron (2001), WorldCom and Global Crossing (2002) and Parmalat (2003), whose actions went unchecked by auditors and boards
Financially engineered products such as derivatives were sometimes used to disguise how bad the failing firms' positions were
The US responded with legislation (SOX); England instead used corporate codes and "comply or explain"
The 2007-2009 global financial crisis was the epitome of risk management failure
Describe best practices for the governance of a firm's risk management processes
Explain the risk management role and responsibilities of a firm's board of directors
Evaluate the relationship between a firm's risk appetite and its business strategy, including the role of incentives
Illustrate the interdependence of functional units within a firm as it relates to risk management
Assess the role and responsibilities of a firm's audit committee

risk-governance.name: Risk Governance

risk-governance-infrastructure.definition: The structures through which a firm links corporate governance to risk management and pushes risk policy down to business managers.

value: Are corporate governance best practices related to best practice in risk management, and if so, how?
How is risk management delegated through the organization?
What roles do executive staff and board committees play in executing and overseeing risk management?
How does risk management policy filter down to business managers and show up in regular business?

risk-governance-infrastructure.name: Infrastructure of Risk Governance

risk-management-building-blocks.definition: Ten building blocks of risk management; most "disasters" associated with risk management are caused by the failure to recognize them.

value: The risk management process
Identifying risk: knowns and unknowns
Expected loss, unexpected loss, and tail loss
Risk factor breakdown
Structural change: from tail risk to systemic crisis
Human agency and conflicts of interest
Typology of risks and risk interactions
Risk aggregation
Balancing risk and reward
Enterprise risk management (ERM)
Explain the concept of risk and how risk management differs from risk taking

risk-management-building-blocks.name: Risk Management Building Blocks

risk-management-process.definition: The high-level cycle a risk manager follows: identify, analyze, manage, and assess the impact of risks.

value: Identify: name, categorize, understand
Analyze: rank, score, measure, and quantify
Manage: avoid, retain, mitigate, or transfer
Assess impact: effects, knock-ons, repercussions
Avoid risks by discontinuing the business or pursuing it with a different strategy
Retain risks within the firm's risk appetite, e.g. via risk capital allocation, self-insurance or captive insurance
Mitigate risks by reducing exposure, frequency, and severity
Transfer risks to a third party using derivatives, structured products, or by paying a premium
Evaluate and apply tools and procedures used to measure and manage risk

risk-management-process.name: Risk Management Process

risk-management-roadmap.definition: The sequence of questions a firm should answer to manage risk, from identifying its risk appetite through implementing and regularly re-evaluating its approach.

value: Identify risk appetite: key corporate goals and risks, whether and which risks to manage, a broad risk appetite statement
Map risks and make choices: measure risk and impact, run risk/reward analysis (e.g. RAROC), choose a basic strategy
Operationalize risk appetite: risk policies, a risk limit framework, and a right-sized risk management team
Implement: choose tactics and instruments, make day-to-day decisions, establish oversight
Re-evaluate regularly to capture changes in risk appetite, business activity, the risk environment and new tools
Compare strategies a firm can use to manage its risk exposures and when each is appropriate

risk-management-roadmap.name: Risk Management Roadmap

risk-management-strategy-selection.definition: After defining and prioritizing the most important exposures, a firm weighs the costs and benefits of retaining, avoiding, mitigating or transferring each risk.

value: Retain: accept a risk in its entirety or part of a loss distribution
Avoid: risks regarded as "unnatural" to the business; some firms have a zero-tolerance policy
Mitigate: e.g. asking for additional collateral, or an airline buying more efficient aircraft to reduce jet fuel exposure
Transfer: pass some portion of risk to third parties
Compare strategies a firm can use to manage its risk exposures and when each is appropriate

risk-management-strategy-selection.name: Strategy Selection: Retain, Avoid, Mitigate, Transfer

risk-mapping.definition: Identifying risks at the level of cash flows and timing, which the high-level risk appetite does not show.

value: E.g. mapping a manufacturer's future copper needs to understand its commodity price exposure
For foreign exchange risk, first map existing positions, contracts and upcoming transactions, then set a hedging policy
Some exposures need insuring, such as natural disasters, physical mishaps and cyber incidents

risk-mapping.name: Risk Mapping

risk-transfer-toolbox.definition: The instruments a firm can use to transfer financial risk to the risk management markets, mainly swaps, futures, forwards and options, chosen to fit the situation and the risks each instrument brings.

value: A key difference is trading mechanics, exchange-traded versus private bilateral OTC agreements
OTC and exchange-based instruments differ in liquidity and counterparty credit risk
Managers combine OTC and exchange-based instruments into a huge variety of strategies
Risk management began with agricultural futures listed on the CBOT in the 1860s
Busch managed commodity price risk with aluminum, corn and rice swaps, sugar and wheat futures, and energy and plastic derivatives
Airlines cannot simply raise ticket prices when fuel costs rise, so they hedge jet fuel with swaps, call options and collars
Unhedged American Airlines benefited from the 2014 fall in jet fuel prices while hedged competitors did not
Assess the impact of risk management tools and instruments, including risk limits and derivatives

risk-transfer-toolbox.name: Risk Transfer Toolbox

risk-versus-uncertainty.definition: Frank Knight and John Maynard Keynes distinguished measurable risk, which can be quantified with statistics, from uncertainty, which cannot be quantified at all.

value: Risk is measurable; uncertainty is not
Rumsfeld: known knowns, known unknowns, and unknown unknowns
Nuclear war is a possibility, but its likelihood cannot be quantified
Frank Knight, Risk, Uncertainty and Profit (1921)

risk-versus-uncertainty.name: Risk versus Uncertainty

sarbanes-oxley-act.definition: US federal legislation passed after the early-2000s corporate failures (Enron, WorldCom, Global Crossing) that enforces corporate governance rules through stricter securities regulation.
sarbanes-oxley-act.name: Sarbanes-Oxley Act

sox-key-provisions.definition: The main obligations SOX places on publicly traded companies and their CEOs and CFOs around accurate reporting and internal controls.

value: CEOs and CFOs ensure reports filed with the SEC are accurate
CEOs and CFOs affirm that disclosures give a complete and accurate picture of the company's financial condition and operations
CEOs and CFOs are responsible for the design and maintenance of internal controls
The effectiveness of reporting procedures and controls must be reviewed annually
The names of board audit committee members must be disclosed

sox-key-provisions.name: Sarbanes-Oxley Key Provisions

specific-market-risk.definition: The risk that an individual asset will fall in value more than the general asset class.
specific-market-risk.name: Specific Market Risk

strategic-risk.definition: Risk from large, long-term decisions about the firm's direction, major investments of capital, human resources, and management reputation.

value: Banks deciding whether to build FinTech services internally, acquire FinTech companies, or partner with them

strategic-risk.name: Strategic Risk

stress-testing.definition: Imagining a plausible worst-case scenario that may develop in stages over an extended period; it focuses on severity rather than frequency.
stress-testing.name: Stress Testing

supervisory-review-and-evaluation-proces.definition: A European regulatory response to the 2007-2009 financial crisis.
supervisory-review-and-evaluation-proces.name: Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process

swap.definition: A derivative contract through which two parties exchange the cash flows or liabilities from two different financial instruments.

value: The most common are interest rate swaps, e.g. swapping a fixed interest rate for a variable one to hedge against rising rates
Airlines use swaps to hedge jet fuel prices

swap.name: Swap

systemically-important-financial-institu.definition: Under Dodd-Frank, a bank holding firm with more than USD 50 billion in assets. SIFIs are regulated by the Federal Reserve.
systemically-important-financial-institu.name: Systemically Important Financial Institution

systemically-important-markets-and-infra.definition: An element of the Basel III macroprudential overlay. For OTC derivatives, the Basel Committee is pushing the market to move as many trades as possible through central clearing and trade reporting.
systemically-important-markets-and-infra.name: Systemically Important Markets and Infrastructures

tail-risk.definition: Very rare and extreme events, which may arise from unobserved structural changes in a market. They are difficult to identify, but a long time series of data should reveal evidence of them.

value: Subprime mortgage lending in the early 2000s and its contribution to the global financial crisis

tail-risk.name: Tail Risk

theta.definition: An option greek: the change in option value as the option expiration date approaches.
theta.name: Theta

three-lines-of-defense.definition: A way of organizing risk oversight into the business line, specialist risk managers, and independent assurance.

value: First: the business line that generates, owns and manages risk
Second: risk managers who specialize in risk management and day-to-day oversight
Third: periodic independent oversight and assurance, such as internal audit
Explain how conflicts of interest can impact risk management

three-lines-of-defense.name: Three Lines of Defense

tier-1-capital.definition: The sum of common stock, retained earnings and certain reserves.
tier-1-capital.name: Tier 1 Capital

total-loss-absorbing-capital.definition: Standards that apply to global systemically important banks (G-SIBs); one of the five elements of the Basel III macroprudential overlay.
total-loss-absorbing-capital.name: Total Loss-Absorbing Capital

typology-of-risks.definition: The classes of risk a firm faces and the way they flow into one another.

value: Market and credit risks are a natural part of a bank's risk structure; risk scales with reward
More operational risk does not lead to greater reward, so banks avoid it when they can
Risk types interact, e.g. an operational risk leads to a dangerous market position that ultimately ruins reputation
Mismatching price movements are typically a bigger problem than any single market risk exposure
A credit portfolio is riskier with fewer large loans, positively correlated defaults, and positively correlated EAD, PD and LGD
Describe the key classes of risk, how each arises, and its potential impact on an organization
Explain how risk factors interact with each other

typology-of-risks.name: Typology of Risks and Risk Interactions

unexpected-loss.definition: The extent to which losses depart from the average (expected) loss level.

value: A portfolio with one very large loan defaulting versus a large number of small loans
Commercial real estate losses that follow regular boom-and-bust cycles

unexpected-loss.name: Unexpected Loss

value-at-risk.definition: The loss over a set horizon that will not be exceeded with a given confidence level, under normal market conditions.

value: Needs three inputs: confidence level, horizon, and a loss distribution
Can be estimated parametrically, by historical simulation, or by Monte Carlo
Fails to capture risk in the tail of the loss distribution; expected shortfall addresses this
Helps compare the risk exposures of different business lines
Popular for risk aggregation, but was never calculated with one set methodology, so use it with caution
parametric-var
Define VaR and explain its limitations as a risk measure

value-at-risk.name: Value at Risk

volcker-rule.definition: The Dodd-Frank provision, proposed by former Fed Chairman Paul Volcker and effective July 2015, that bans banking entities from proprietary trading and from owning or partnering in hedge funds and private equity funds.
volcker-rule.name: Volcker Rule
